newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: No need for quick Swiss gold sales - government.
newsitem.headline: No need for quick Swiss gold sales - government.

text.p: Switzerland is in no hurry to sell official gold reserves that will be left over for projects even after transfering gold to a proposed seven billion Swiss franc humanitarian foundation, a finance ministry official said on Friday.

Parliament will decide what to do with around seven billion Swiss francs in revalued gold that will remain available after transferring an equal amount to the foundation, ministry director Ulrich Gygi told a news briefing

At issue is a rise of around 14 billion Swiss francs in the value of Swiss National Bank gold reserves that is expected from plans in Berne to lift a 1971 law fixing their price at 4,595 francs per kg, about a third to a quarter of the current market value.

Swiss President Arnold Koller on Wednesday said Berne wanted to use half of this new wealth to create a foundation for aiding the poor and persecuted, which would sell the gold gradually and invest the money for interest to run its operations.

Asked what the government planned to do with the remaining seven billion in revalued gold, Gygi said there were a number of proposals taking shape in parliament for uses ranging from deficit reduction to social security.
"It is up to parliament to decide what to do with the profit from revaluation," he said, but added there was no need to sell the gold quickly.
"As for the second tranche of gains from the revaluation, there is no need to realise its value immediately by selling it," he said. "We will be able to wait for the market" to develop, he added.
Both the foundation and the revaluation of gold reserves are part of a complex package of legislation that the government hopes to have approved by parliament next year.
Under the Swiss system of direct democracy, key parts of the package will have to be approved by voters in a referendum which the government also plans to schedule sometime in 1998.

Gygi acknowledged that gold markets were sensitive to sales at the moment because of recent reductions in official reserves by some European central banks, such as those in Belgium and the Nwetherlands.
"Here we have to be very, very cautious," he said, but he gave no more details.

Swiss National Bank (SNB) spokesman Werner Abegg stressed that the proposed "Swiss Foundation for Solidarity" would have no interest in pushing down gold prices by selling its stock quickly after it comes into being in late 1998 or early 1999.

"It is in the basic self-interest of the foundation that gold prices do not tumble, that it be able to preserve its capital," Abegg told the joint news conference with Gygi and other government officials.
SNB Chairman Hans Meyer has said the foundation could sell the gold it gets over 10 years to avoid market disruptions.
The foundation could then spend some 300 to 400 million Swiss francs a year from interest on investmnents made with the cash from gold sales, accoridng to the government proposal.
